title: Acceptance of artificial intelligence among pre-service teachers: a multigroup analysis
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines what factors shape pre-service teachers’ acceptance and intended use of AI-based educational applications, and whether these relationships differ by gender. The authors frame the problem as an important but under-studied issue in teacher education, especially as AI tools such as ChatGPT and related educational applications become more visible in schooling. They argue that understanding acceptance among future teachers is important because their attitudes may influence how AI is adopted in classrooms later on.

The study used a questionnaire grounded in Technology Acceptance Model 3 (TAM3), measuring AI self-efficacy, perceived enjoyment, AI anxiety, perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, subjective norm, job relevance, and behavioral intention. Data were collected online from 452 pre-service teachers at one German university enrolled in teacher education programs. The analysis used structural equation modeling, measurement invariance testing, latent mean comparisons, and multigroup analysis to examine both overall relationships and gender differences.

Results showed that perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use were the strongest predictors of intention to use AI, with perceived usefulness having the larger effect. AI self-efficacy and perceived enjoyment predicted perceived ease of use, while subjective norm and job relevance predicted perceived usefulness. AI anxiety did not significantly predict perceived ease of use in the full sample, but gender moderated some paths: female participants reported higher AI anxiety and the anxiety-to-ease-of-use path differed by gender, as did the ease-of-use-to-usefulness path. The authors conclude that teacher education should address AI-related anxiety, especially among female pre-service teachers, and should emphasize the practical usefulness and usability of AI tools.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed cross-sectional survey with structural equation modeling and multigroup invariance testing, but it is correlational and does not evaluate an intervention or causal effect. The evidence is methodologically solid for acceptance modeling, yet it lacks experimental manipulation or direct outcome measurement in classrooms.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has unclear direct impact on K-12 learning outcomes because it measures pre-service teacher acceptance rather than student achievement or implementation effects. Its main contribution is institutional and preparatory, informing future adoption of AI in education rather than demonstrating measurable educational impact.

interventions.use_case: Survey-based acceptance of AI-based educational applications among pre-service teachers, using TAM3 constructs (AI self-efficacy, perceived enjoyment, AI anxiety, perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, job relevance, subjective norm, behavioral intention); no specific AI tool was deployed.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that pre-service teachers’ AI acceptance was shaped by affective and self-belief factors, but anxiety was not a direct predictor of behavioral intention. AI self-efficacy positively predicted perceived ease of use (β=0.359, p<0.001; n=452), while perceived enjoyment also positively predicted perceived ease of use (β=0.518, p<0.001). AI anxiety did not significantly predict perceived ease of use (β=-0.037, p>0.05), and gender differences showed higher AI anxiety among female pre-service teachers (z=-3.217, p<0.01).
finding.measure: TAM3 survey constructs: AI anxiety, perceived enjoyment, AI self-efficacy, perceived ease of use, behavioral intention

finding.finding_summary: The paper found strong positive associations between perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and intention to use AI-based educational applications. Perceived usefulness was the strongest predictor of behavioral intention (β=0.501, p<0.001), followed by perceived ease of use (β=0.297, p<0.001); together, SN, PE, and PEOU explained 65% of the variance in behavioral intention (R²=0.65).
finding.measure: Behavioral intention to use AI-based educational applications; TAM3 structural equation modeling

finding.finding_summary: The study provides evidence relevant to teacher education institutions by showing that AI acceptance among pre-service teachers is measurable and gender-invariant at the configural, metric, and scalar levels, with only partial strict invariance requiring one freed item. Gender significantly moderated two paths in the model: AI anxiety to perceived ease of use (female β=-0.119 vs male β=0.254; Δχ²=5.638, p=0.018) and perceived ease of use to perceived usefulness (female β=0.530 vs male β=0.283; Δχ²=9.987, p=0.002).
finding.measure: Measurement invariance and multigroup SEM by gender
finding.effect_size: ΔCFI=0.011 for strict invariance rejection; Δχ²=5.638 and 9.987 for moderated paths
